Arrest means to stop something completely and hold it in place. This single core idea runs through every use of the word — whether it's a person, a process, or even attention.
Meaning 1: To seize and detain a person by legal authority

This is the most common meaning. When law enforcement arrests someone, they forcibly stop that person from going free and take them into custody — meaning they hold them under their control.

"The police arrested the man outside the store."
"She was arrested on suspicion of fraud."
"They arrested him and took him to the station."

A few important things to understand about this sense:

  • It requires authority. In most situations, only a law enforcement officer can legally arrest someone. The act is backed by the law.
  • Being arrested does not mean being guilty. It only means the person has been stopped and detained because there is enough reason to suspect they may have committed a crime. The legal process to determine guilt comes later.
  • The person loses their freedom of movement. They cannot simply walk away. They are held — this is the "stopping and holding" idea made literal.
  • You will often see the phrase "placed under arrest" or "taken under arrest," which means the same thing.
  • Someone who has been arrested is "under arrest" — a phrase the officer may say directly to the person.
Meaning 2: To stop a process from continuing

This is a slightly more formal or technical use, very common in medicine, science, and journalism. Here, the "thing being stopped" is not a person, but a process — usually something harmful or negative that is actively happening or spreading.

"Doctors worked quickly to arrest the bleeding."
"The new drug helped arrest the spread of the infection."
"Urgent action is needed to arrest the decline of the forest."
"The treatment arrested the progression of the disease."

Notice the pattern: you "arrest" the spread, the growth, the decline, the bleeding, the progression — things that are in motion and need to be stopped.

This sense does not always mean something is reversed or cured — it means it is brought to a halt, stopped from getting worse.
Meaning 3: To catch and hold someone's attention

This is a more literary or expressive use, but it appears regularly in writing and educated speech. When something arrests your attention (or your gaze), it grabs you so powerfully and completely that you cannot look away or move on — you are, in a sense, "stopped in your tracks."

"The painting arrested my gaze the moment I entered the room."
"A sudden loud sound arrested everyone's attention."
"There was something about her presence that arrested him."

This is not violent or negative — it simply means something was so striking, so powerful, or so unexpected that it fully captured you. The word suggests the hold is total, not partial.
The thread that runs through all three meanings

Every use of arrest carries the same underlying idea: something that was moving, progressing, or flowing freely is brought to a firm, complete stop and held there.

  • A person is stopped from moving freely → arrested by police
  • A disease is stopped from progressing → arrested by medicine
  • A wandering gaze is stopped from moving on → arrested by something beautiful or striking

This is why the medical term cardiac arrest (which is a noun, but worth knowing) means the heart has stopped beating — it has been "arrested."

• arrest someone → police take them into custody
  • arrest the spread / growth / decline / bleeding / progression of something → stop a process
  • arrest someone's attention / gaze → powerfully capture and hold their focus
  • be under arrest → currently detained by law enforcement
  • place/put someone under arrest → formally detain them

The word carries a sense of force and totality. You don't use arrest for a gentle slowdown. If something is merely slowing, you'd say "slow" or "reduce." Arrest means a complete stop, held firm. That firmness is built into the word.
